Support DECIMAL widths up to 255 digits, stored as BIGNUM blobs

DECIMAL(width, scale) with width > 38 now stores its unscaled value as a BIGNUM blob
(PhysicalType::VARCHAR). The BIGNUM encoding is order-preserving, so comparisons, sorting,
MIN/MAX, hashing, joins, zonemaps (string statistics) and storage work on wide decimals
without decimal-specific code. Fixed-size decimals up to 38 digits are unchanged, and results
only become wider than 38 digits when one of the inputs already is.

Adds casts to and from wide decimals (strings, integers, hugeints, floating point, booleans,
BIGNUM and fixed-size decimals, with rounding and range checks), + - * % and unary - through
BignumIntermediate, SUM/first/last/arg_min/arg_max/abs, Value support, CSV and JSON reading,
and clear NotImplemented errors for AVG, round/ceil/floor/trunc, Parquet and the Appender,
which previously fell through to the HUGEINT code path. Also adds DECIMAL -> BIGNUM casts and
makes the three statistics sites that assumed numeric types carry NumericStats check the
statistics kind instead.

Test and tidy the first/last string state after widening alloc_size

The previous commit widened FirstStringStateBase::alloc_size to idx_t so that
NextPowerOfTwo(len) is no longer truncated to 0 for strings longer than 2^31
bytes, which made Allocate(0) hand out a zero-length region that the following
memcpy wrote gigabytes past. Reachable from first(), last() or any_value() on a
VARCHAR or BLOB.

On top of that, drop the remaining uint32_t cast on len (string_t::GetSize
already returns idx_t, and the cast belongs at the string_t constructor) and
record on the field why it has to be wider than uint32_t.

This mirrors the fix that landed for the same defect in SuffixFunction.

The added test exercises the allocation-reuse branch that alloc_size governs -
growing, shrinking and regrowing - since the truncation itself needs a
multi-gigabyte string to trigger and cannot be covered in an ordinary test.

aggregate: widen FirstStringStateBase::alloc_size to idx_t to stop the 2GB integer truncation

FirstStringStateBase::Assign() stored the arena allocation size in a
uint32_t after casting NextPowerOfTwo(len). For any input string with
len in (2^31, 2^32-1] -- a size DuckDB s own string_t cap permits --
NextPowerOfTwo returns 2^32, and the outer UnsafeNumericCast to uint32_t
truncates that to 0. Release builds then Allocate(0) and memcpy(len)
bytes past the returned stub, producing an attacker-controlled heap
buffer overflow reachable through any first()/last()/any_value() over
a VARCHAR or BLOB column. Debug builds crash at the checked cast.

Widen alloc_size to idx_t so NextPowerOfTwo s uint64 result survives.
The field s doc comment already notes it is not part of the exported
state; the four extra bytes only touch the aggregate s internal state
layout. The alloc_size >= len reuse check keeps working because len is
promoted to idx_t at the comparison.

Expand aggregate state export to work with lists (`StateListType`) and sort keys (`StateSortKey`), and add aggregate state export to `list`, `any_value/first/last`, `arg_min/arg_max` (#23199)

Follow-up to https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/23186

This PR extends the aggregate state export functions to allow for
automatically exporting lists and sort key-serialized values, which are
commonly used in aggregate functions in particular for complex nested
types. These types can now be defined using the same state layout, and
are automatically (de)serialized into states without requiring extra
per-aggregate code to support the state layouts.

### Lists

Lists can be defined using the `StateListType`, and operate on the
`LinkedList` structure that we use to efficiently store lists of
arbitrary data in the `list` aggregate. This is what the `list`
aggregate state looks like now:

```cpp
struct ListAggState {
	using STATE_TYPE = StateListType<StateReturnType>;

	LinkedList linked_list;
};
```

`StateReturnType` is a special marker that says "the logical type of
this element is equivalent to the return type of the aggregate
function".

This is what the exported aggregate state looks like:

```sql
select list({'a': i, 'b': date '2000-01-01' + interval (i) days}) export_state as list_state from range(3) t(i);
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                     list_state                                                     │
│                                                  aggregate_state                                                   │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ [{'a': 0, 'b': '2000-01-01 00:00:00'}, {'a': 1, 'b': '2000-01-02 00:00:00'}, {'a': 2, 'b': '2000-01-03 00:00:00'}] │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The `LinkedList` structure is automatically traversed and (de)serialized
to the structured aggregate state object, as part of the aggregate state
export.

### Sort Key

Similarly, sort keys are used in `first/last/any_value` and
`arg_min/arg_max` when dealing with complex (nested) objects. Objects
are serialized to a `string_t` blob using the sort key format, and
deserialized again when the final result is constructed. The
`StateSortKey` template is added which adds generic support for
(de)serializing such structures. For example, here is what `first` looks
like:

```cpp
struct FirstSortKeyState {
	static constexpr const char *STATE_NAMES[] = {"value"};
	using STATE_TYPE =
	    OptionalStateType<StructStateType<OptionalStateType<StateSortKey<StateReturnType, OrderType::ASCENDING>>>>;

	string_t value;
	//! Whether the recorded value is valid (i.e. not NULL)
	bool value_is_valid;
	//! Whether the state has been set (i.e. we have seen a row)
	bool is_set;
	//! The size of the arena allocation for a non-inlined string value - not part of the exported state
	uint32_t alloc_size;
};
```

`first` is interesting because it has two layers of optionality - as the
value can also be set to `NULL`, i.e. the following two values are
different:

```sql
-- single "NULL" value provided
select first(null) export_state value_set_to_null;
┌───────────────────┐
│ value_set_to_null │
│  aggregate_state  │
├───────────────────┤
│ {'value': NULL}   │
└───────────────────┘
-- no value provided
select first(null) export_state empty_value from range(0);
┌─────────────────┐
│   empty_value   │
│ aggregate_state │
├─────────────────┤
│ NULL            │
└─────────────────┘
```

The two layers of `OptionalStateType` and the two booleans account for
this.

The actual sort key is specified by `StateSortKey<StateReturnType,
OrderType::ASCENDING>` - which looks for a `string_t` and then uses the
sort key helpers to (de)serialize it to construct the aggregate state:

```sql
select first({'a': 42, 'b': 84}) export_state as state;
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│             state             │
│        aggregate_state        │
├───────────────────────────────┤
│ {'value': {'a': 42, 'b': 84}} │
└───────────────────────────────┘
```

Cardinality estimator: don't let a one-sided distinct count shrink the join domain

The join domain is picked by tier (HLL/exact count, then min/max span,
then row count), not by size. When only one side of a join key has a
strong count, e.g. a native fact joined to a CSV, range() or multi-file
Parquet dimension, the fact's few distinct keys become the domain and
the join is over-estimated by dimension keys / fact keys (40x for a
fact's 1,824 dates against a 73,049-row date dimension).

Let a weaker bound from the other side raise the domain: a scan
column's row count (if it has no usable distinct count or span), or its
min/max span capped at the rows left after filters. The bound must be
larger than the strong count and no larger than the smallest relation
behind it; the smallest such bound wins. Computed columns, unions with
a computed branch, and LIMIT outputs don't qualify.

This assumes the side without a count is a key. If it isn't (e.g. a CSV
or Parquet VARCHAR fact on the same keys), or if two tables with counts
join through one such dimension, the join is under-estimated.
